query: For magnetic high-entropy alloys, what single intervention could increase the coercive field? State one testable hypothesis that specifies the intervention, the mechanism expected to alter coercivity, the predicted outcome relative to a matched baseline, the conditions under which the effect should hold, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing nanoprecipitates into magnetic high-entropy alloys will increase the coercive field by acting as domain wall pinning sites, thereby hindering domain wall movement and enhancing magnetic hardness.
generation.conditions: room temperature, standard magnetic field testing conditions
generation.mechanism: domain wall pinning and magnetic domain structure
generation.baseline: low coercive field in as-cast or annealed magnetic high-entropy alloys
generation.boundary: limited to room temperature and standard magnetic field testing conditions
generation.uncertainty: effect of nanoprecipitate size and distribution on coercive field

falsification_experiment.design: prepare magnetic high-entropy alloy samples with and without nanoprecipitates, measure coercive field at room temperature
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if coercive field does not increase with introduction of nanoprecipitates, hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: To gain further insight into the coercivity mechanism, angular dependence of the coercivity as a function of RTA time has been measured and well‐fit to a model based on domain wall displacement (Figure S5, Supporting Information), indicating a pinning‐controlled coercivity for the in‐plane direction.[  ] The evolution of fitting parameters also reveals significant deviations in the overall demagnetization factors from the thin film geometry after RTA, even before film dewetting, reflecting the change in anisotropy induced by RTA. Therefore, the hard magnetic properties in FeCoNiMnCu film may be explained by RTA‐induced microstructure changes and anisotropy enhancement which strengthens domain wall pinning.

By tracking the Bloch walls’ movement under different applied magnetic fields (yellow dashed area in Figure 3c), we see that the domain's growth is relatively smooth within the grains while it appears to be pinned at the grain and twin boundaries. This observation confirms that the coherent nanoscaled L12 precipitates do not exert notable magnetic pinning forces on the domain walls’ movement, in any case very small when compared to those at grain/twin boundaries.[  ] The Figure S6, Supporting Information shows a schematic representation of the Bloch wall pinning mechanisms for the HEAs with different precipitate sizes.

Therefore, it can be inferred that the grain boundaries in these HEAs are not acting as a deteriorating factor for the relatively low H c (<11 Oe) required for soft magnetic applications.[  ] The slightly increased H c observed for the Al‐doped HEAs (Figure 3b) is mainly associated with the increasing volume fraction of the L12 phase (Figure 4a) and the corresponding lattice misfit (Figure 4b). Nevertheless, according to the in‐situ observations of domain wall movement (Figure 3c), the pinning effect on the Bloch walls movement exerted by the precipitates is insignificant compared to that from high angle and twin boundaries.

The coercivity increases when the domain wall movement is impeded by the microstructural discontinuities and sharp gradients.[  ] Therefore, the abundant microcracks in the CoCrFeNithin film would form a discontinuous interface for the magnetic flux, change the magnetic field distribution, and increase the leakage magnetic field above the cracks.[  ] Moreover, the microcracks can reinforce the pinning effect of the domain walls. Hence, the coercivity of the CoCrFeNithin film is larger than that of the CoCrFeNithick film. To eliminate the influence of the defects on the coercivity, we analyzed the relationship between the coercivity and the microstructure of the films without microcracks. According to the technical magnetization theory,[  ] H C is mainly related to the defect‐induced irreversible movement of the domain walls as well as the irreversible rotation of the magnetic moments, which are influenced by the magnetic anisotropy. Nanocrystalline soft magnetic materials exhibit a single domain structure owing to the small crystal grain sizes, and there is no domain‐wall movement during the magnetization‐reversal process.
